notes.notes: Good morning. I want to tell you about a fishing town of 1,900 people on the coast of Maine, a place called Port Alder. It has a harbor, a general store, a grange hall, a lobster co-op, and a lot of weather. If you drove through it on a summer afternoon, you would not slow down. Nothing about Port Alder is special, and I want you to hold on to that, because that's the point. This is not a story about a rich town, or a town full of engineers, or a town with a pile of federal money. It is a story about ordinary people who got tired of waiting and decided to keep their own lights on. I'll walk you through what happened to them, what they built, what nearly stopped them, and what it gave them back. And I'll be honest about my motive. By the end, I hope you'll want to go home and do what they did, with your own neighbors. So let me start with the autumn when that harbor went quiet and cold.

It started with a storm. On October 9th, 2023, Storm Elsa came up the coast and took down the only transmission line into town. One line. That was the whole connection between Port Alder and the grid, and when it fell, there was no second way in. People expected a day, maybe two. Instead it was eleven days before power came back. Think about what eleven days means in a fishing town in October. The co-op's freezers failed on day two. Forty thousand pounds of lobster spoiled, and that is not just food, that is a season's income for families who live boat to boat. The cold came into the houses, and two elderly residents were hospitalized from it. Folks ran generators until the fuel ran out, then ran extension cords from neighbors who still had some. The church opened its doors at night. Everyone did what they could, and everyone waited for the line to be fixed somewhere far away by someone they had never met. When the lights finally came back, the town was relieved, but it was also angry, and it was asking a question. And the answer it reached was not really about wires at all.

Those eleven days could have just been a bad memory. What turned them into something else was a realization, and nobody put it better than Ruth Calloway, the harbor master. Ruth said this to me in her kitchen, a year after the storm, with a cup of coffee going cold in front of her. She wasn't blaming the storm, and she wasn't really blaming the utility either. What she was saying is that the town already had everything it needed. It had the people, people who repair engines and wire boats and run a co-op through bad years. It had the roofs, big flat ones on the co-op and the school and the store. It had the will, because nobody wanted to watch another freezer full of lobster go bad. What it didn't have was anyone telling it that a town could build its own power. Power was something that arrived from somewhere else, and when it stopped arriving, you waited. That is the real outage Ruth was naming, and I think most of our towns are living in it right now, whether the lights are on or not. We wait for permission that nobody is coming to give. That sentence is the hinge of this whole story, because once Port Alder heard it out loud, the waiting stopped. And then the town did something nobody expected of a place its size.

Once they stopped waiting, things moved fast. In January 2024, sixty people packed the grange hall on a cold weeknight: three hundred households sending their people, one fishing co-op, and no experience at all. Nobody there had built anything bigger than a boat shed. And they voted 58 to 2 to try. I love that number, because it tells you two things. The town wanted this badly. And there were doubters, who were allowed to say no and stay in the room. A project like this lives or dies on whether the whole town owns it. But a vote is only a promise, and next came turning a show of hands into money and panels.

So they had a vote and a lot of nerve. What they needed next was everybody else, and I want to show you how a town talks itself into something as strange as a power plant, because it happened in three seasons. The first phase was door-knocking. In spring 2024, twelve volunteers visited every house in Port Alder. Not a mailing, not a website, a person on your porch. The feeling in that phase was hopeful but unsure, and the question in every volunteer's head was simple: will anyone sign up? Then summer came, and the answer turned out to be yes. By summer, 312 households had pledged, and a state resilience grant matched them, which brought the total to $2.1M. For a town of that size, that is an enormous number, and it came mostly from kitchen tables. That's when the mood changed. People started saying this might actually work, out loud, at the store and on the docks. Then winter. In December, the first panels went up on the co-op roof, in a snowstorm, of course, because this is Maine and nothing there comes easy. People stood in the parking lot to watch them bolted down, and the feeling was close to elation. The thought on everyone's mind was we did this ourselves. Notice that the arc here is emotional as much as technical. The panels were the easy part. The hard part was getting from hopeful but unsure to proud. And that pride would be tested very soon, because the next year was not kind to them.

That pride on the co-op roof did not last long without a fight. Twice in one year, the project nearly died, and I want to walk you through both times, because this is the part most stories about community energy skip. In January 2025, the utility denied the interconnection permit. Their lawyers said a fishing co-op couldn't be a power company, that this was not the kind of thing towns get to do. Imagine you are one of those volunteers who knocked on every door. You have the money, you have the panels, and now you are told it was never allowed. Then, in March 2025, nature took its turn. An ice storm cracked the first battery enclosure, and we lost two months. Two months of winter, of wondering whether the whole thing had been a mistake. Some people stopped coming to meetings. But the town kept going. In June 2025, the state court sided with the town and ruled the co-op may sell power to its members. That ruling opened a door for every small co-op in the state. And then, in September 2025, came the moment I still think about. We cut the line to the grid on purpose. That is an islanding test: you disconnect from the outside world and see whether you can stand alone. And the lights stayed on. Both near-deaths were survived the same way, by people refusing to quit. But I skipped over something in March. The ice storm didn't just cost them time. It cost them money they did not have.

When that battery enclosure cracked, the damage was not only to the schedule. The project was $412,000 short, and the ice storm had put them there. For a project funded mostly by households, that is the kind of gap that ends things. So they did what you are supposed to do. They went to the bank, and the bank said no. They went to the state, and the state said wait. Wait was the one word this town had decided never to accept again. So the co-op put a jar on the counter at the general store. Not a campaign, not a fund with a logo, just a jar by the register with a handwritten card. And 140 neighbors covered it in nine days. Fishermen, retirees, teachers, people who had already pledged in the summer and came back to give again. That's the moment I knew this would work. Not when the panels went up, not when the court ruled. It was the jar. A town that closes a gap like that in nine days has already decided the project belongs to them. Money from outside can be withdrawn. Money from your neighbors comes with their stubbornness attached. And with that gap closed, the batteries went in, and the harbor started to change in ways you could see from the water.

So the jar did its job, the batteries went in, and the harbor itself began to look different. Let me describe the before and after, because it is easy to talk about microgrids in the abstract. Before the microgrid, the harbor ran on hope and diesel. The town saw 31 hours of outages a year, and every dock had a diesel generator on it, loud and smoky and expensive, waiting for the next storm. If you fished out of Port Alder, part of your budget went to fuel just to keep the lights and pumps going when the line went down. And the line always went down. Today the town sees 2 hours of outages a year, and the harbor runs on sun and storage. The batteries carry the harbor through anything short of a direct hit. That is the co-op's phrase, and they mean it. The generators are still there, by the way. Nobody tore them out. But nobody has started one in a year. They have become a kind of museum of the old way of living with power, a reminder of what used to be normal. People forget quickly how bad things were. The numbers do not forget, and on a chart the change is almost hard to believe.

Those idle generators tell the story one way. This chart tells it another, and it is the chart I show every town council. It comes from the Port Alder Power Co-op: outage hours fell from 286 to 2 in three years. That spike is 2023, the storm, those eleven days in the dark and the cold. Then look at what happens after. Since the microgrid came online, outages have all but disappeared. In 2026, the town was without power for 2 hours in the whole year. When I show this to councils, the room goes quiet, because every one of them has their own spike in memory. What this line says is that the spike does not have to repeat. It is not weather that decides how long a town sits in the dark. It is preparation. But if you take away only this line, you will miss what actually changed in Port Alder.

That chart is about hours, and hours are what engineers care about. But what the town got back was more than electricity, and the people there will tell you that first. Start with the power itself. 62% of the town's electricity is now made in town, on its own roofs, stored in its own batteries. The money that used to leave town for fuel and bills mostly stays. Households save $340 a year on average, and in a fishing town that is real money, a month of groceries or a set of new traps. Then there is the test nobody planned for. When Storm Nadia hit in 2026, Port Alder was dark for 0 hours. It was the only lit town on the peninsula. Neighboring towns sat in the dark, and people drove into Port Alder to charge phones and keep medicine cold. The town that once waited eleven days for help became the place others came to for help. Think about what that does to how a community sees itself. And it did not stop at the town line. 14 towns have asked for the playbook. They are not asking about panels. They are asking how Port Alder got organized, how it found the nerve, how it held together through the lawsuit and the ice. Which brings me to what I actually came here to tell you, the idea underneath all of these numbers.

Those towns asking how are asking the right question. And this is what I came here to say. We talk about resilience as infrastructure: wires, poles, substations. Things a utility installs and a crew repairs. All of that matters. But in Port Alder, resilience was neighbors who had done something hard together and knew they could again. It was the volunteers on the porches, the people in the grange hall, the jar on the counter. Every town has the people for that. What few towns have is someone telling them they are allowed to start, the very thing Ruth said was missing. Resilience cannot be delivered to a town from outside. It has to be built by the people who live there, and the building is what makes it last. So the question for you is not whether, but where to begin.

So if resilience is built by neighbors, let me give you a way to start building it, and I mean next month. There are four steps, and none of them needs an engineer. The first is to map. List the buildings that must never go dark. In Port Alder that was the clinic, the school, and the store with the freezers. You already know what is on your list, and writing it down makes the project real. The second step is to gather. Find your twelve, the people who will knock on doors. Every town has them. They run the bake sale, coach the team, show up at the meeting. You need twelve who will not give up. The third step is to ask. Request the interconnection study before you need it. Ask early, because it takes a year, and you want that clock running while you are still knocking on doors. Port Alder learned the hard way how much the paperwork matters; you can learn it from them. And the fourth step is to build, but small. Start with one roof and one battery. Not a master plan, just one proof that your town can do this. Once people see it working, the rest of the town follows. Every one of these steps begins with the same thing, and it is the last thing I want to leave you with.

Those four steps all begin with people, and that's where I want to end. Port Alder didn't have money. It didn't have expertise. It didn't have permission, and for a long time it didn't think it was allowed to ask. What it had was twelve people willing to knock on doors, and neighbors who answered. Everything else, the panels, the court ruling, the jar on the counter, came after that. So here is what I'm asking of you. Go home and find yours. Look around your town for the people who show up, and ask them to knock on a few doors with you. You do not need anyone's permission. The playbook is free, at portalderpower.org/playbook. Go find your twelve. Thank you.
